title.en: Law of radioactive decay, half-life and mean life

hook.en: Nobody can say which kernel will pop next, yet a full pan pops in a predictable way. Single nuclei decay at random, but a large number decay by a precise law.

objectives.en: State the law of radioactive decay
Use N = N₀e^(−λt), half-life and mean life

narration.en: Nobody can say which kernel will pop next, yet a full pan pops in a predictable way. Single nuclei decay at random, but a large number decay by a precise law.

body.en: The rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei: $dN/dt = -\lambda N$, where λ is the decay constant. Integrating, $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. The activity $R = \lambda N = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ is measured in becquerel (1 Bq = 1 decay per second; 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq). The half-life is $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda \approx 0.693/\lambda$ and the mean life is $\tau = 1/\lambda \approx 1.44\,T_{1/2}$.

Each dot decays at a random moment, yet the fraction left follows the dashed curve. Every half-life, half of what is left decays.

prompt.en: After 12 s, exactly one-eighth of a sample is left. Set the half-life and lock in.

explanation.en: 1/8 = (1/2)³: 12 s is three half-lives, so T½ = 4 s.

body.en: Count half-lives: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 after 1 to 5 half-lives. 1/10 left takes about 3.3 half-lives; 1/100 about 6.6; 1/1000 about 10.
